paras.title: One line is enough
paras.text: Someone types: I'm bored. Most apps ask what you want. This one starts from who you are, and what tonight is like.

paras.title: A search box or a cousin?
paras.text: Planning a night out? A search box needs you to know what you want, then you pick from a long list. Or you could ask an older cousin, who already knows you. She says: you like calm, so try the quiet thali place.

paras.title: Or say it exactly
paras.text: Veg dinner for 4 tonight, under ₹500 each. Something sweet on the way home. Back by 10. The app splits it into what to find, what must hold, and what you like.

paras.title: Ideas go out from home
paras.text: Now the city. Three ideas go out from Home.

paras.title: Every idea is checked
paras.text: The rooftop grill is ₹1,400 each. Over budget. The beach shack has no veg menu. Every idea is checked against what you said must hold.

paras.title: One becomes the route
paras.text: Kaveri thali place passes. Dinner at 7:30, then dessert at Malli at 9:05. Leave at 7:15. Back by 9:40.

paras.title: A reply, not a list
paras.text: It comes back like a message from a friend. Where to eat, what it costs, and when you are home. It ends by offering a change.

paras.title: Different from the apps you know
paras.text: Google Maps answers a search. It waits until you know. Booking apps sell a table once you have decided. The Cousin starts before the search.

paras.title: Early numbers
paras.text: In a simulation with 50 synthetic people, the full design had 71% of first replies accepted. A simple nearest open place app had 40%. No product code exists yet. Real friends have to confirm these numbers.

paras.title: Why it is built this way
paras.text: The AI is the voice, not the brain. The AI listens and explains. Code chooses, checks and remembers.

paras.title: Takeaway
paras.text: A cousin who knows you, knows the city, and always has a good idea.

paras.title: One sentence, five stages
paras.text: One sentence goes through five stages. Each stage makes the list of places smaller, so the slow, costly steps only see a handful.

paras.title: Planning a dinner for friends
paras.text: Say you plan a friends' dinner yourself. First, work out what they asked for. Cross off places that can't work. Pick favourites from the rest. Fit the evening together, in order. Then phone to check they're open.

paras.title: Understand
paras.text: Stage one: understand. The AI cuts the sentence into pieces, and gives each a type. Two things to find. Four rules. One taste.

paras.title: Narrow
paras.text: Stage two: narrow. About 3,000 places near you. The rules apply one by one. Veg. Open. Seats 4. Fits the budget. Leaves time to get home. About 40 are left.

paras.title: Rank
paras.text: Stage three: rank. Each of the 40 is scored on long-term taste from the notebook, plus tonight. The best six dinner places and six dessert stops go forward.

paras.title: Combine
paras.text: Stage four: combine. Google gives the travel times between those 12 places and home. A route solver keeps the best pair that gets you home before 10.

paras.title: Check
paras.text: Stage five: check. Every rule is checked again, on fresh data. Then code prints each name, price and time. The AI only writes the reasons.

paras.title: Why the Cousin does it this way
paras.text: So the slow steps only ever see 12 places, not 3,000. The AI listens. Code chooses and checks. All of it takes about a second.

paras.title: Takeaway
paras.text: Five stages. Each one makes the list smaller.

paras.title: Must-haves and nice-to-haves
paras.text: Some things are must-haves: yes or no. Others are nice-to-haves: they get a score. We call the rules fences, and the scores magnets.

paras.title: Choosing a flat to rent
paras.text: Renting a flat? The fences: pets allowed, under ₹25,000 a month, within 30 minutes of work. Fail one, and it's out.

paras.title: Magnets rank the rest
paras.text: Magnets rank the rest, by sunlight and a nice balcony. The gorgeous one doesn't allow pets, so it stays out.

paras.title: In the app: veg dinner for 4
paras.text: Veg dinner for 4, under ₹500 each, home by 10. 150 places could serve dinner. Fences first. Fail one, and the place is out, however good it is. Vegetarian. Under ₹500, from our own cost bands. Seats 4. Open at 7:30. Home by 10.

paras.title: Magnets score what is left
paras.text: Magnets next. The thirty left are scored for this person tonight.

paras.title: The top six go forward
paras.text: The top six move on to the next stage.

paras.title: No way back through scoring
paras.text: This place isn't veg, but its taste score is very high. It tries to come back, and bounces off. Nothing that broke a fence can ever come back through scoring.

paras.title: Why the Cousin works in this order
paras.text: So in the Cousin, a rule is never traded for taste. And the expensive steps only see six dinner places, not 150.

paras.title: Takeaway
paras.text: Fences remove. Magnets rank. They never mix.

paras.title: Three ideas, not one idea three times
paras.text: Pick the three best scores, and you can get three near-copies. A better reply is one sure thing, one a little new, one surprise.

paras.title: Planning a Sunday for a friend
paras.text: A friend visits on Sunday. Your top three ideas are all beach walks. Better: a beach walk, a new cafe, and a pottery class they would love.

paras.title: In the app: every idea is a circle
paras.text: Every place that passed the fences is a circle. Alike places sit close. Bigger means a better match tonight.

paras.title: Plain ranking takes the three biggest
paras.text: Plain ranking takes the three biggest. Zoom in: all dosa or thali places. The same evening, three times.

paras.title: The mix starts with a safe bet
paras.text: The mix picks a safe bet first: the best match. Everything similar to it shrinks, since being like a pick already made is less useful.

paras.title: Then a stretch, then a wild card
paras.text: Next, a stretch: still a strong match, a little newer. Then a wild card: new to them, but still fitting their taste. A random far-off pick is rejected. Random is never allowed.

paras.title: Three different evenings
paras.text: Safe, stretch, wild.

paras.title: Ask for more, and the mix runs again
paras.text: Three is the default, not the limit. Say show me more. The mix runs again on the same shortlist of about 40 places. Every rule still applies.

paras.title: Or ask for ten
paras.text: Say give me 10 options: a short list, best first, but spread out. Code fills in each row's facts.

paras.title: When nothing is left
paras.text: Any others, with nothing left? The fence stays put. That's all that fits. Raise the budget to ₹600 and there are four more. The fences never loosen on their own.

paras.title: Why the Cousin mixes
paras.text: So you never get one idea three times. A list stops at about 10. Past that, it asks what to change.

paras.title: Takeaway
paras.text: Three good ideas, not the same idea three times. Ask, and there are more.

V05.title: The route puzzle and evening arc

paras.title: The best pair, not the two best
paras.text: The best dinner and the best dessert may not work together. So we pick the best pair, not the two best.

paras.title: Lunch, then a film, home by 5
paras.text: Say you want lunch, then a film, and be home by 5. Your favourite lunch and favourite film are far apart, so that pair gets you home late. The best pair that fits has a different lunch.

paras.title: In the app: the stops
paras.text: Tonight: the three dinner ideas, and the top three dessert stops, each with a score.

paras.title: Travel times between every pair
paras.text: One request to Google gives the travel time between every pair. Google can't choose stops. It only measures.

paras.title: The solver tries every combination
paras.text: The solver tries each dinner with each dessert: 9 combinations.

paras.title: Late, or a big detour: out
paras.text: A plan that gets home late is out. So is a plan where dessert is a big detour. Dessert must be on the way home.

paras.title: The best total score wins
paras.text: Among the plans that fit, the best total score wins.

paras.title: Dessert comes after dinner
paras.text: Order matters too. Dessert comes after dinner. A plan with the sweet first is marked down.

paras.title: The plan: dinner, dessert, home
paras.text: Dinner at 7:30, dessert at 9:05, home by 9:40. That leaves a traffic buffer before 10.

paras.title: Why the Cousin works this way
paras.text: In the Cousin, Google measures and code chooses. The AI only writes the reasons around the plan.

paras.title: Takeaway
paras.text: The best evening is a set of stops in the right order.

paras.title: A favourite needs a rest
paras.text: A favourite is a good pick. The same favourite every week is not.

paras.title: A song you love, on repeat
paras.text: Play a song you love all week, and by Friday you are tired of it. Rest it for a few weeks, and it is a joy again.

paras.title: In the app: the same place again
paras.text: You loved Kaveri thali place last Saturday. Without a rest, its high score makes it the safe bet again, and again.

paras.title: A rest penalty that fades
paras.text: So every place you visit gets a rest penalty, and it fades over time. A place you loved is back in rotation after about a month.

paras.title: Loved, liked, disliked
paras.text: One you only liked rests longer, about two months. One you disliked is never suggested again.

paras.title: Clubs are the opposite
paras.text: Going back is the goal, so a club you liked gets a small bonus instead.

paras.title: You can always override it
paras.text: Say "take me back to Kaveri", and that is a pin. Pins beat the rest.

paras.title: Why the Cousin works this way
paras.text: A rest keeps ideas fresh without dropping what you love. And the pin keeps you in charge.

paras.title: Takeaway
paras.text: A place you loved should rest before it comes back.

paras.title: Remember slowly, notice quickly
paras.text: A good memory forgets slowly. One odd night shouldn't erase what you really like. But when your life changes, it should notice fast.

paras.title: A friend who always orders coffee
paras.text: Think of a friend who always orders filter coffee. One Friday she has tea. You don't rewrite what you know about her. But if she says, I've quit coffee, you update at once.

paras.title: In the app: late nights
paras.text: Take another line in the notebook. Four weeks in, it says this person loves late nights, and their outings prove it. Then life changes. They start early gym. Nobody tells the app. The notebook line barely moves. Fading is slow on purpose, so one bad night can't erase a real taste.

paras.title: Way 1: listening
paras.text: Way one is listening. They mention it in passing: joined a gym, up at 5 now. The line is replaced at once.

paras.title: Way 2: a monthly catch-up
paras.text: Way two is a monthly catch-up. One 20 second question: still into late nights? In the test, it caught 95% of changes.

paras.title: Way 3: a surprise meter
paras.text: Way three is a surprise meter. It counts the ideas the person passed on. Alone, it was slow: it caught 31% of changes, about 5 weeks late.

paras.title: Why the Cousin does it this way
paras.text: So the notebook fades slowly, to protect a real taste. Listening comes first, and a monthly catch-up checks. The meter only brings the catch-up forward.

paras.title: Takeaway
paras.text: Remember slowly. Notice change quickly.

paras.title: A surprise that learns
paras.text: A wild card is a surprise: something new that might still suit you. But which kinds of surprise do you actually enjoy? The app finds out by trying, gently.

paras.title: Which stall to try on Friday?
paras.text: Say a food street has three stalls. You know stall A well: you've loved it 6 times out of 8. You know B a little, and C not at all. Where do you go? Mostly A. But now and then C, because it might be even better.

paras.title: In the app: five kinds of surprise
paras.text: In the app, there are five kinds of surprise. For each kind, a belief curve shows how much the app thinks you'd enjoy it. At first it knows nothing, so every curve is flat.

paras.title: One round, step by step
paras.text: Each round, it draws a random guess from every curve: a small triangle. It tries the kind with the highest guess. Loved it pushes that curve to the right. Not for me pushes it to the left.

paras.title: Forty rounds, quickly
paras.text: Now watch 40 rounds. As evidence piles up, the curves get narrower. That means more certain. Dawn trips keep missing, so they're tried less. But being unsure still earns them an occasional chance.

paras.title: What was true all along
paras.text: Now the hidden truth for this person, in dashed lines. The curves landed close. It found what works for them without being told.

paras.title: Why the Cousin does it this way
paras.text: Always picking the favourite would miss better things. Picking at random would waste evenings. So it tries good bets more often, and still gives unsure ones a chance.

paras.title: Takeaway
paras.text: Surprises that learn what you like.

paras.title: Ask only when it matters
paras.text: Every question costs the person a moment. So the app asks only when the answer changes the plan. Four outcomes: fill silently, don't ask, guess out loud, ask.

paras.title: Ordering pizza for friends
paras.text: Ordering pizza for friends? You know she loves mushroom, so you just order it. Paper plates or steel? It changes nothing, so you don't ask. Any allergies, with 10 guests? A wrong guess ruins the evening, so you ask.

paras.title: In the app: three gates
paras.text: Each missing detail passes three gates. Do we already know? Would it change the picks? Is a wrong guess costly?

paras.title: Budget wasn't said
paras.text: Say tonight's message left out the budget. The notebook says about ₹600, so it fills it in silently.

paras.title: Seats for 4?
paras.text: Seats for 4? Every place left seats 4, so asking changes nothing.

paras.title: Spice level
paras.text: Spice matters, but a wrong guess is easy to fix. So it guesses out loud: I've assumed medium spice.

paras.title: Indoor or outdoor?
paras.text: Indoor or outdoor? Tonight's picks come out the same, so it doesn't ask.

paras.title: Now imagine: we're 10
paras.text: Now imagine: we're 10. A budget guess changes the picks, and a wrong one spoils a group dinner. So it asks.

paras.title: At most one question
paras.text: The rule: at most one question per reply. The AI only words the question. Code decides whether to ask.

paras.title: Why the Cousin does it this way
paras.text: So most gaps are filled quietly. You are asked only when it truly matters.

paras.title: Takeaway
paras.text: Ask only when the answer would change the plan.

paras.title: One message, many asks
paras.text: One message can hold several asks. Some are fine. Some are not. A good answer judges each ask on its own.

paras.title: A friend asks for two favours
paras.text: A friend texts: drive me to the airport at 6 am, and sit my exam for me. You don't refuse the whole message. Airport? Yes, happy to. Your exam? No. But I'll help you revise.

paras.title: In the app: one message
paras.text: Now the app. Someone writes: biryani at my friend's wedding, then a bike race late at night, back by 5 am. Give that one combined score, and the three asks blur together. So the Cousin judges each piece separately.

paras.title: Three pieces, six lanes
paras.text: The message splits into three pieces, and each piece gets its own checks. Every piece ends in one of six lanes. Serve it. Swap in a safer version. Or ask a question. Or say no: can't, won't, or not ours.

paras.title: Piece one: the wedding biryani
paras.text: Piece one: biryani at someone's wedding. Is it safe? Yes. Is it in scope? No. It's a private event. So it lands in not ours. But the wish for wedding-style biryani is kept.

paras.title: Piece two: the bike race
paras.text: Piece two: a bike race late at night. Is it safe? No. It's a street race. So it lands in won't. But a safe version comes back: a karting track.

paras.title: Piece three: back by 5 am
paras.text: Piece three: back by 5 am. Safe? Yes. In scope? Yes. Fits? Yes. So it's served, and the plan is built around it.

paras.title: The reply goes piece by piece
paras.text: A clear no where one is needed, and something real to do instead. Wedding-style biryani, karting, and home by 5.

paras.title: Why the Cousin does it this way
paras.text: One unsafe ask never sinks the rest. Verdicts come from typed checks. Scores only rank what is allowed.

paras.title: Takeaway
paras.text: Say no to the piece, not the person.

paras.title: Reasons and facts
paras.text: Anything said about a place has two kinds of words. A reason is an opinion: calm, proper thali. A fact can be checked: a price, a distance, the hours.

paras.title: One wrong fact
paras.text: A friend says: go to that thali place, calm and lovely, open till 11. You arrive at quarter past 10. It closed at 10. An AI can make the same slip, in a lovely sentence. One wrong fact breaks trust for good.

paras.title: In the app: IDs and reasons
paras.text: In the app, the AI hands back only an ID and a reason. Nothing else. No name, no price, no hours.

paras.title: Code prints the facts
paras.text: Code takes that ID to the fact store. It prints the name, the price, the distance and the hours itself.

paras.title: Only the reason is the AI's
paras.text: Only the reason line comes from the AI. A wrong opening time can't come from it, because it never writes one.

paras.title: A checker scans the reason
paras.text: One more safeguard. A checker scans the reason for stray numbers or names. Say the AI slipped in: open till 11. The checker finds it, and deletes it.

paras.title: The card the person sees
paras.text: Checked facts from data, and a reason that sounds human.

paras.title: Why the Cousin does it this way
paras.text: An AI can't get a fact wrong if it never writes one. And if one slips into a reason, the checker removes it.

paras.title: Takeaway
paras.text: Code prints the facts. The AI writes the reasons.

V12.title: Who is called, in what order

paras.title: Who is called, in what order
paras.text: For one reply, the Cousin calls a few outside services. Each does one job. Our own code makes every decision.

paras.title: Planning a day out
paras.text: Planning a day out, you might ask a friend to put it in words, look up distances on a map, and check your own notes. They give you information. You make the choices.

paras.title: You ask, the app reads
paras.text: You send one sentence. The app reads your notebook from our own data.

paras.title: Claude splits, Google lists
paras.text: Claude splits the sentence: two things to find, four rules, one taste. Google Places lists dinner and dessert spots. We keep their IDs, not copies. Our data adds the confirmed facts.

paras.title: Our code decides
paras.text: Now our own code decides. Fences and magnets cut 3,000 to 12. No service is asked to choose. Google Routes measures every trip between those 12 places and home, in one call.

paras.title: Solve, then explain
paras.text: The route solver and the checks leave one plan. Claude is called again, only to write the reasons.

paras.title: The plan comes back
paras.text: Google draws the road path and the map pins. The plan reaches you: 7:30, 9:05, home by 9:40.

paras.title: Why the Cousin does it this way
paras.text: That is about two AI calls and a handful of Google calls per reply. Everything else is our code, so the decisions stay ours.

paras.title: Takeaway
paras.text: Google knows the city. We know the person. Code decides.

V13.title: The whole machine: every algorithm, one evening

paras.title: Every algorithm, one evening
paras.text: Every video so far showed one piece. Here they all work together, on one evening.

paras.title: A kitchen on a busy night
paras.text: In a busy restaurant kitchen, the order is read, and anything off the menu is turned away. The cooks work in order. The head chef checks every plate before it leaves. Each person does one job, in one order. The Cousin works the same way.

paras.title: Stage 1: understand
paras.text: Saturday. You and three friends send one message. First, the AI listens, and fills in the card. Two things to find. Four rules: veg, four people, ₹500 each, home by 10. One taste: South Indian, calm. Each piece of the message is checked. All three are fine, so everything is served. Should it ask? The budget was said, and the rest is known. So no question.

paras.title: Stage 2: narrow
paras.text: Stage two narrows. About 3,000 places are near you. Gather keeps the dinner and dessert places. Then five fences, one by one: veg, open, seats 4, fits the budget, home in time. About 40 are left.

paras.title: Stage 3: rank
paras.text: Stage three ranks. Magnets score the 40 on taste from the notebook, plus tonight. If you had been somewhere recently, it would be resting, and slide down.

paras.title: Stage 3: safe, stretch, wild
paras.text: The mix picks a safe bet, a stretch and a wild one. Places too like a pick shrink. The wild one comes from the kinds of surprise you enjoy. Six dinner places and six dessert stops go forward.

paras.title: Stage 4: combine
paras.text: Stage four combines. Google measures the travel times between the 12 places and home. The solver tries the pairs, drops late plans and detours, and keeps dessert after dinner. The safe plan: Kaveri at 7:30, Malli at 9:05, home by 9:40.

paras.title: Stage 5: check
paras.text: Stage five checks. The rules are checked again, on fresh data. Code prints the name, price, distance and hours. The AI writes the reasons, and a checker strips any stray fact.

paras.title: The reply: three ideas
paras.text: The reply: the safe plan in full, a newer idea, and a surprise. About two AI calls in all. Everything else is code.

paras.title: Sunday: how was Kaveri?
paras.text: Sunday morning, the Cousin asks: how was Kaveri? You say: loved it. That becomes a tentative line in the notebook, and Kaveri starts its rest. The next plan starts a little smarter.

paras.title: The card keeps track
paras.text: People change their minds mid-chat. The card has three boxes: what to find, what must hold, and what you like. Each new message changes only part of it.

paras.title: Message 1: a new plan
paras.text: Message one: veg dinner for 4, with something sweet on the way home. No card yet, so the AI writes one, and every stage runs. The reply: Kaveri at 7:30, Malli at 9:05, home by 9:40.

paras.title: Message 2: a change of taste
paras.text: Message two: make it livelier. Only the likes line changes. Search and rules are reused. Ranking and the rest run again.

paras.title: Message 3: a question
paras.text: Message three: is the thali place open late? The card doesn't change. The answer is a fact we already fetched, so only explain runs.

paras.title: Message 4: show me more
paras.text: Message four: show me more. Understand and narrow are reused, and so are the rank scores. The mix step picks three new ideas, not the three already shown. Combine, check and explain run again, with fresh facts. Quick, because the search and the ranking are skipped. Give 10 options, and the card gets a count of 10.

paras.title: Message 5: scrap and restart
paras.text: Message five: scrap it, we're 10 now. Find and the group size change. Veg and home by 10 are carried over, said aloud. One question first, because a budget for 10 changes the picks. Then a fresh search.

paras.title: Message 6: choose
paras.text: Message six: let's do the second one. Find becomes dinner, chosen. Planning ends. The plan goes to the map, and tomorrow the learner asks how it went.

paras.title: Why the Cousin works this way
paras.text: Each algorithm does one job, at one step, in one order. The AI listens and explains. Code decides, checks and remembers.

paras.title: Takeaway
paras.text: One message, five stages, every piece in its place.

V14.title: The ladder: when data grows, the models

paras.title: Rules first, models later
paras.text: A rule is written by hand: if this, then that. A model learns from examples. With few examples, rules are safer. With many, a model can spot more.

paras.title: A new tea stall
paras.text: A new tea stall has no customer history, so the owner uses a rule of thumb. Strong tea for office workers, ginger for evening walkers. A year on, her notebook shows patterns that no rule of thumb caught.

paras.title: Try it on half first
paras.text: She tries the new idea on half her customers first. It sells more, so it wins. If it sold less, the old rule stays.

paras.title: Some jobs are never learned
paras.text: Adding up the bill has one right answer, so it is never learned.

paras.title: In the app: day one, 50 people
paras.text: Day one, 50 people. The AI model listens and explains. The rest is code and rules.

paras.title: Around 1,000 people
paras.text: Around a 1,000, embeddings match places by feel, statistics sharpen the ranking, and wild cards become a bandit.

paras.title: Around 5,000 people
paras.text: Around 5,000, trees may take over ranking, but only if they win a live test.

paras.title: The live test decides
paras.text: Half the evenings use the rule, half use the trees. The winner takes the cell. If the trees lose, the rule stays.

paras.title: Many cities: 50,000 people
paras.text: In many cities, a smaller tuned AI and OR-Tools join. Deeper models may help rank and track taste, only where they win.

paras.title: Two rows stay code
paras.text: Fences and facts, and the route solver: they have right answers, so they stay code.

paras.title: Why the Cousin climbs this way
paras.text: So the Cousin starts with rules it can trust. A model has to earn its place with a live test.

paras.title: Takeaway
paras.text: Start with rules. Earn each model with a live test.

paras.title: A habit that happens outside the app
paras.text: Some apps want your time on the screen. The Cousin wants a habit around going out: once or twice a week.

paras.title: Like a weekly cricket game
paras.text: Think of a weekly cricket game with friends. A ping on Thursday, and a yes from everyone. You play, with the phone in your pocket. Next day, you laugh about the best moment.

paras.title: In the app: six steps, then again
paras.text: Thursday evening, a nudge, when people plan the weekend. One line is enough to get a plan. Friends vote and commit. A plan with a time and a yes is far more likely to happen. Then the phone goes dark, and the city lights up. Next day, a recap card. People remember the best moment and the ending. The notebook grows, so the next plan is a little better.

paras.title: We count outings
paras.text: We don't count minutes in the app. We count outings.

paras.title: Why the Cousin does it this way
paras.text: The reward happens out in the city, not on the screen. So the app asks for little, and each outing makes the next plan better.

paras.title: Takeaway
paras.text: The reward is the evening, not the screen.

paras.title: A wheel that speeds up
paras.text: A flywheel is a heavy wheel. Hard to start, but every push adds to its speed. In a business, each turn of the loop feeds the next.

paras.title: A neighbourhood tailor
paras.text: Every fitting goes into a book of measurements. Next time the fit is better, so customers return and bring friends.

paras.title: A rival opens across the road
paras.text: A rival can copy the sign and the scissors. Not the book.

paras.title: In the app: every outing teaches us
paras.text: Every outing tells us something Google doesn't know. Who went, with whom, and whether they loved it.

paras.title: The Cousin's flywheel
paras.text: More outings give more outcome data. That makes the next picks better, for you and for people like you. Better picks earn more trust, and trust brings more outings. Each turn is a little faster than the last.

paras.title: What a competitor can copy
paras.text: A competitor copies the features. Buttons and screens clone across. But the wheel holds three things that can't be copied: years of outcomes, confirmed facts, and clubs.

paras.title: Why the Cousin is built this way
paras.text: So the Cousin keeps a record of how every evening went. The longer it runs, the further ahead it gets.

paras.title: Takeaway
paras.text: Features can be copied. Years of evenings can't.

paras.title: One weekend, start to finish
paras.text: Planning a weekend usually takes effort. Let's follow one, from Thursday to Sunday, with just one sentence of effort.

paras.title: A group chat, or one sentence
paras.text: Think of planning dinner in a group chat. Where? Who's veg? What time? It goes on and on. Now imagine saying it once, and getting a plan back.

paras.title: Thursday evening
paras.text: One well-timed nudge, not a feed to scroll.

paras.title: Saturday: one sentence
paras.text: One sentence is the whole input. Veg dinner for 4 tonight, under ₹500 each. Something sweet on the way home. Back by 10.

paras.title: A checked plan in about a second
paras.text: A checked plan comes back in about a second. Kaveri at 7:30, Malli at 9:05, home by 9:40. Every fact is printed from data.

paras.title: Friends join the plan
paras.text: Friends join the plan, and three say they are in. A plan with people who said yes is far more likely to happen.

paras.title: Checked again before you leave
paras.text: Before you leave, hours and traffic are checked again. Still open. 12 minutes away.

paras.title: Then the evening happens
paras.text: Then the evening happens, out in the city, not on the screen.

paras.title: Sunday morning
paras.text: One question: how was Kaveri? The answer becomes a tentative note in the notebook.

paras.title: Thursday to Sunday at a glance
paras.text: That is the whole weekend, with one sentence in the middle.

paras.title: Why the Cousin does it this way
paras.text: Places change, so facts are checked again just before you go. And one evening isn't proof, so the note stays tentative.

paras.title: Takeaway
paras.text: Thursday to Sunday, with one sentence in the middle.
